records.title: Organ-on-a-Chip Technology in Otorhinolaryngology: Design Strategies and Applications in Mucosal Tissues and Head and Neck Cancer.
records.abstract: The complex mucosal microenvironment of the upper aerodigestive tract influences otorhinolaryngologic diseases. Therefore, establishing preclinical models that recapitulate the structural and functional characteristics of otorhinolaryngologic tissues is important for understanding disease pathophysiology and evaluating therapeutic responses. Recently, organ-on-a-chip (OoC) has emerged as a promising in vitro approach to address limitations of conventional models. OoC can reproduce key tissue-level features under controlled microenvironmental conditions by integrating relevant cell or tissue sources, spatial organization, dynamic culture conditions, and multicellular interactions. In this review, we focus on representative OoC applications in oral mucosa and gingiva, nasal mucosa and airway, and head and neck cancer (HNC). We discuss how OoC design strategies are tailored to the intended biological or preclinical application and summarize the current applications, translational challenges, and future directions of these models. Continued advances in patient-relevant model development, reproducibility, standardization, and validation against in vivo and clinical findings may further strengthen the role of OoC as a complementary preclinical platform in otorhinolaryngology.

records.title: NCLX Inhibition plus Ca2+ Delivery Potentiates Electroporation and Antitumor Immunity in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
records.abstract: Irreversible electroporation (IRE) is increasingly used for locally advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet electric-field heterogeneity leaves a low-field rim where residual cells survive, and recurrence is frequent, compounded by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Here, an electroporation-synchronized adjuvant strategy is developed that integrates intratumoral Ca2+ delivery with nanoparticle-mediated inhibition of mitochondrial NCLX using CGP37157 (mPEG-PCL@CGP37157). This regimen markedly enhances cytotoxicity in PDAC cell lines and patient-derived organoids and significantly improves local control and survival in syngeneic subcutaneous and orthotopic PDAC models, without overt systemic toxicity. Reduced therapeutic efficacy in T cell-deficient hosts demonstrates the importance of adaptive immunity. Mechanistically, EP-resistant PDAC cells upregulate NCLX to buffer mitochondrial Ca2+ stress. Concurrent Ca2+ delivery and pharmacological NCLX inhibition induce sustained mitochondrial Ca2+ overload, triggering immunogenic GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis. This is accompanied by enhanced dendritic cell activation and CD8+ T-cell responses, as well as suppression of a tumor-myeloid SPP1-CD44 axis, promoting pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization. Collectively, targeting NCLX potentiates the immunogenic effects of IRE and provides a translatable strategy for eliminating residual disease in PDAC.

records.title: The VCPIP1-UBE3A Deubiquitination-Ubiquitination Cascade Contributes to Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer Progression.
records.abstract: The molecular mechanisms underlying progression from metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) to metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remain incompletely understood. Paired proteomic profiling of specimens from 10 patients identified VCPIP1 as a candidate regulator, and its clinical relevance was evaluated in an independent cohort of 128 mHSPC patients. Elevated VCPIP1 expression was independently associated with shorter CRPC-free survival. Functional studies demonstrated that VCPIP1 promoted prostate cancer proliferation, migration, invasion, and metastasis in a deubiquitinase activity-dependent manner. Mechanistically, VCPIP1 directly bound UBE3A and stabilized it by removing K48-linked polyubiquitin chains at Lys711, thereby enhancing UBE3A-mediated p53 ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Wild-type UBE3A, but not its catalytically inactive C833A mutant, rescued the malignant phenotypes suppressed by VCPIP1 depletion. TP53 knockdown partially reversed these effects in TP53-wild-type LNCaP cells but not in TP53-mutant DU145 cells, indicating a TP53 context-dependent contribution of p53. VCPIP1 depletion also reduced androgen receptor expression in LNCaP cells and enhanced enzalutamide sensitivity in patient-derived organoids. These findings identify a VCPIP1/UBE3A deubiquitination-ubiquitination cascade contributing to CRPC progression and support further investigation of VCPIP1 as a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target.

records.title: Theratyping for personalized medicine across cystic fibrosis disease models.
records.abstract: In the era of CFTR modulators, cystic fibrosis (CF) is being profoundly reshaped for treatment-eligible individuals. Theratyping, an ex vivo strategy assessing individual responses to CFTR modulators, supports precision medicine, particularly for rare variants where conventional trials are limited. In this Review, we discussed advances in CF disease modelling, highlighting strengths, limitations and translational relevance. We also outlined future directions aligned with the Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement (3 R) ethical principles in animal research, including organ-on-a-chip technologies, to improve mechanistic insight and preclinical predictivity. CF research offers therefore a paradigmatic framework for therapeutic innovation in other rare genetic diseases.

records.title: Reprogramming of Metabolic and Adipokine-related Gene Expression in 3D Mammary Epithelial Organoids by Dietary Bioactive Compounds.
records.abstract: Dietary bioactive compounds can modulate mammary gland gene expression, potentially influencing milk composition and infant metabolic programming. This study investigated whether selected dietary bioactive compounds modulate leptin and adiponectin expression in rat mammary epithelial organoids (MEO), a 3D in vitro model of the mammary gland. 18 nutrients were initially screened for effects on leptin gene expression, followed by confirmatory and dose-dependent analyses focusing on oleic acid (OA), leucine (Leu), betaine (Bet), and their triple combination. mRNA levels of leptin, adiponectin, and β-casein (Csn2), as well as selected genes related to one-carbon and lipid metabolism and specific microRNAs, were analyzed. OA, alone or in combination, consistently increased leptin, adiponectin, and Csn2 mRNA expression in MEO compared with controls. These effects were accompanied by downregulation of lipogenic markers, including Srebp1, and increased Cpt1b expression under the triple-combination treatment, without significant changes in miRNA levels. In contrast, Bet and Leu showed more variable, context-dependent effects on leptin, adiponectin, and Csn2 expression, while altering miRNA profiles that differed from those observed under OA-containing treatments. Overall, the results indicate that dietary bioactive compounds modulate gene expression of rat MEO.

records.title: ARHGEF2 isoform switching couples intestinal epithelial barrier function with autophagic host defense response to pathogens.
records.abstract: Intestinal epithelial integrity is essential for host defense, yet how epithelial junctional scaffolds coordinate antimicrobial immunity remains unclear. We show that the long GEF-H1 isoforms (mouse Arhgef2-207; human ARHGEF2-219) localize to adherens junctions in polarized epithelial cells through interactions with actin and Nectin-3, whereas the shorter Arhgef2-201 isoform localizes to tight junctions. Conditional deletion of epithelial Arhgef2-207 induces Arhgef2-201 expression, disrupts barrier integrity, activates autophagy, and causes small-intestinal inflammation. In human intestinal organoids, Listeria monocytogenes selectively depletes junction-associated ARHGEF2-219, triggering a switch to ARHGEF2-201 and RhoA- and STING-mediated autophagic signaling. This transition coincides with loss of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and epithelial polarity. Here we show that a pathogen-induced ARHGEF2 isoform switch links junctional perturbation to autophagic responses and immune activation, revealing a mechanism that couples barrier disruption to cell-intrinsic antimicrobial defense.

records.title: Virtual cells: progress and challenges from mechanistic modeling to data-driven integration.
records.abstract: Virtual cells aim to represent cellular states computationally and predict responses to genetic, chemical, environmental, temporal, and spatial conditions. For comparative purposes, this review uses state encoding (E), state transition (T), and observation decoding (D) as a conceptual abstraction spanning explicit mechanistic models, data-driven foundation and perturbation models, multimodal systems, and spatial and multiscale simulation. We examine model boundaries, data foundations, resource disclosure, out-of-distribution evaluation, causal evidence, and experimental validation. Independent benchmarks show that parameter count and training-set size do not automatically yield robust out-of-distribution generalization, while transcriptomic representations alone do not capture the full functional state of a cell. Trustworthy virtual cells will require perturbation-responsive transitions, cross-modal alignment, continuous-time dynamics, mechanistic constraints, calibrated uncertainty, independent experimental validation, and, where appropriate, closed-loop experimental feedback.

records.title: Progress of metabolomics-centric multi-omics research in medicine.
records.abstract: Metabolomics reveals molecular changes at the metabolic level during biological processes. Recent advancements, particularly through integration with other omics and artificial intelligence (AI), are advancing metabolic data analysis and multi-omics interpretation. This review introduces a "metabolomics-centric" paradigm as a conceptual framework for multi-omics integration, positioning metabolic readouts as the functional anchor for interpreting genotype-phenotype relationships. It also chronicles the evolution and medical applications of integration technologies. Our discussion first traces the field's evolution from bulk to single-cell and spatial methodologies, next surveys integration strategies to uncover mechanistic insights, and finally examines how AI-driven multimodal data integration and AI-optimized metabolomics workflows tackle persistent biological and computational challenges. Looking forward, this review identifies the AI virtual cell as a pivotal future direction for metabolomics-based multi-omics integration, calling for increased attention to its development to simulate dynamic molecular phenotypic networks within a multi-omics context.

records.title: Emerging frontiers for AI in single-cell genomics.
records.abstract: We are just over a decade into the single-cell revolution in biology, which has been coupled to the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in single-cell genomics. Most early single-cell RNA embedding models and subsequent "foundation models"-representational models pretrained on large single-cell datasets-did not gain wide traction among experimental biologists. However, as massive single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas efforts ramp up, there is a clear rationale for exploiting AI models to interpret new datasets in the context of vast existing data resources. Meanwhile, the advent of single-cell epigenetic/multiomic assays and Perturb-seq technologies presents new opportunities for AI modeling. Here, we review AI embedding and foundation models for scRNA-seq and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq), extensive machine-learning efforts to exploit single-cell multiome in regulatory genomics, and AI strategies to learn "virtual cell" models from Perturb-seq, ending with a description of current limitations of single-cell AI models and an outlook for future advances.

records.title: Benchmarking biological knowledge-graph priors against single-cell foundation models for Perturb-seq prediction.
records.abstract: Perturb-seq prediction increasingly relies on either biological graph priors or single-cell foundation models, but their relative value is difficult to interpret when architectures, split definitions and graph sources vary simultaneously. We benchmarked STRING functional associations and Gene Ontology co-annotation against dense, self-edge-only and exact-degree-rewired supports in one fixed graph-attention backbone, with a separate 200-HVG STRING-GO-control-co-expression sensitivity. Four public Perturb-seq datasets, three nested gene-space scales and three optimisation seeds were evaluated on held-out guide conditions; GEARS, scGPT and Geneformer were evaluated on the same held-out conditions, output-gene panels and Pearson-r metric after model-specific validity checks. At 200 highly variable genes, STRING-GO improved the equal-dataset Pearson r by +0.016 (95% interval [+0.010, +0.022]) relative to dense support. Dataset effects were positive in Adamson (+0.017), Norman (+0.015), Replogle K562 (+0.017) and Replogle RPE1 (+0.014), and 122/200 guide conditions improved (0.61 [0.54,0.68]). The top-20-gene Jaccard difference was +0.009 [+0.006,+0.012]. STRING-GO exceeded self-edge-only support by +0.024 [+0.018,+0.029] and the mean of ten exact-degree rewires by +0.011 [+0.005,+0.017]. The native-panel effect declined from +0.016 at 200 genes to +0.009 at 1000 genes; the 1000-200 interaction was -0.006 [-0.011,-0.002]. The primary graph-support comparison was formulated and conducted during peer-review revision rather than planned as an a priori confirmatory study. All three external models passed implementation-specific checks. Across 36 protocol-matched dataset-scale contrasts, 32 were within the descriptive ±0.030 reference envelope and four were outside, all favouring the external model. These results demonstrate a modest empirical predictive improvement under the evaluated matched protocol; they do not by themselves establish practical biological relevance.

records.title: AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing: from genome mining to the artificial intelligence virtual cell.
records.abstract: Fungi are important chassis organisms for sustainable biomanufacturing owing to their strong secretion capacity, metabolic diversity, and adaptability to industrial processes. Driven by the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), computational approaches that enable machines to learn patterns from data and make predictions, together with omics technologies and synthetic biology, data- and model-driven strategies are increasingly reshaping fungal cell factory design and optimization. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing, covering AI-assisted genome mining, enzyme and pathway analysis, genome editing, metabolic network modeling, and intelligent fermentation control. The review further highlights the emerging concept of the artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC), which integrates multi-omics data, mechanistic modeling, and machine learning-based approaches into a unified multiscale framework for simulating dynamic cellular behaviors. The technical foundations and potential applications of AIVC in fungal metabolic engineering, drug discovery, agriculture, and environmental biotechnology are reviewed. Finally, key challenges-data quality and standardization, cross-scale model integration and interpretability, and the gap between in silico prediction and experimental validation-are highlighted. This review provides a systematic perspective on the role of AI and virtual cell technologies in advancing next generation fungal biotechnology.

records.title: Programming N-linked glycan composition through de novo protein design.
records.abstract: N-linked glycans are ubiquitous post-translational modifications that mediate diverse biological processes, including cell signaling and adhesion, molecular recognition, and host-pathogen interactions. Despite their importance, N-linked glycans have largely remained beyond the reach of biomolecular design due to a lack of methods capable of jointly modeling glycans and protein structure. Here, we develop a general all-atom computational pipeline for creating de novo glycoproteins in which the amino acid sequence encodes both the location and composition of N-linked glycans. The method uses three-dimensional protein structure to tune glycan accessibility to processing enzymes in the eukaryotic secretory pathway. Systematic increases in steric restriction progressively reduced processing, shifting glycans from heterogeneous complex-type structures toward increasingly underprocessed oligomannose-type species resembling those found on many viral glycoproteins. Despite this programmed restriction, the resulting oligomannose glycans remained accessible for biological recognition, inhibiting uropathogenic Escherichia coli adhesion to human bladder cells and binding mannose-binding lectin. These results establish steric control of N-glycan processing as a genetically encodable design principle and extend computational protein design to functional glycoproteins with programmed composition.

records.title: The physical foundation beneath protein generative modeling.
records.abstract: Physical equations in protein modeling appear to have been replaced by generative models trained directly on structure data. By learning a mapping from noise to data, sampling de novo protein structures has become much more efficient. However, such models can also learn non-physical features and break down with out-of-distribution settings which are typical in protein design campaigns. In this review, we highlight where the physics persists in protein generative modeling pipelines and the issues that linger when physically relevant components of a macromolecular system are left unmodeled. We present a perspective that respecting the underlying physics of macromolecular systems, increasingly through learned representations that are physically grounded and updating generative models with experimental data, is foundational to generative modeling for functional protein design.

records.title: De novo design of ligand binding proteins using large language models alone.
records.abstract: Protein design has rapidly advanced with the advent of sequence- and structure-based machine learning models. However, reasoned design, which applies physicochemical principles and rules derived from sequence-structure-function relationships, has not seen the same benefits from generative machine learning models. Here, we test the ability of common large language models (LLMs; e.g. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini) to consider design principles to generate de novo proteins that bind metals and lipophilic small molecules without copying existing sequences. Common LLMs alone are able to 1) generate protein sequences to adopt a desired fold and bind the target ligand and 2) explain the principles that motivate the design choices. Following structure prediction and filtering, we selected a small set of designs (6 to 12 designs per query) for experimental validation, affording metal binders in one round of LLM-based design (25% hit rate) and perfluorooctanoic acid binders in two rounds (25% hit rate in the second round of design). Importantly, the LLMs produce detailed justification to accompany the de novo designed sequences, providing a conceptual framework on which designs can be evaluated. While the successful designs have some deviations from the prompted parameters and LLM-articulated design rationale, these campaigns provide a case study that highlights the utility of LLMs in making protein design more comprehensible and accessible to users without sophisticated design expertise.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Proteome-Wide Target Prioritization for Drug Discovery against Multidrug-Resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
records.abstract: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes ∼82.4 million infections annually and is rapidly approaching an untreatable status. The pathogen has developed resistance to every antibiotic class introduced since the sulfonamide era. Ceftriaxone, the last WHO- and CDC-recommended empirical therapy, is now compromised by high-level resistance in extensively drug-resistant lineages reported across multiple continents. No licensed vaccine exists, and no antibiotic with a novel mechanism has been introduced for this pathogen in over 40 years. Conventional drug discovery is too slow and insufficiently resistance-aware to address this escalating threat. In this review, we examine in silico proteome-wide target fishing as a rapid, systematic approach. The approach applies six biologically informed filters to the N. gonorrhoeae core proteome: core-genome definition, host-homology exclusion, essentiality screening, metabolic chokepoint identification, subcellular localization, and resistance-aware prioritization. Across data sets spanning 12-69 clinical strains, this pipeline reduces 2000-12,300 protein-coding sequences to 12-30 high-confidence targets. An integrated artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML) scoring layer further ranks candidates using sequence features, AlphaFold2 structures, protein-protein interaction networks, and genotype-phenotype data from ∼20,000 clinical isolates. Five targets showed consistent cross-study prioritization: LpxC, MurA, FabI, DapD, and NGFG_RS03485. Of these, only LpxC has experimental inhibitor validation against multidrug-resistant gonococci; the remaining candidates are supported computationally but lack biochemical confirmation. Bridging this validation gap remains the critical bottleneck. However, advances in pan-genome analysis, structural prediction, and generative AI for compound design provide a more tractable route to novel therapeutics than previously available.

records.title: A Generalized Theory for the Structural and Spatial Mapping of Energy, Entropy, and Free Energy.
records.abstract: Systems in which the free energy density is nonuniform in space are familiar; the surface tension of a water droplet and the surface energy of a solid are good examples. Some such cases can be treated with prior theory, notably inhomogeneous solvation theory (IST), but IST is applicable only to liquids. Despite this limitation, IST has proven useful as a guide to the design of ligands to bind a targeted protein, based on the idea that ligands that displace high free energy water will tend to bind more tightly, other things being equal. Here, we present Generalized Thermodynamic Mapping (GTM) theory, a more general theory that is applicable to the entirety of a biomolecular or other chemical system, and which thus may provide additional guidance for molecular design. For example, it might highlight parts of a ligand whose local free energy rises on binding, thus suggesting where modifications could improve affinity. Starting from classical statistical thermodynamics, we derive structural decompositions that assign energy and entropy to individual atoms or to larger chemical components, such as amino acid residues, and spatial decompositions that define continuously varying thermodynamic densities throughout the system. The potential energy is decomposed via the multibody expansion, and the entropy via the mutual information expansion. The resulting thermodynamic densities satisfy key desiderata: their spatial integrals yield the correct total thermodynamic quantities, the densities vanish where the atomic number density is zero, and all entropy terms above first order go to zero in the absence of correlation. The entropy decomposition in GTM theory is closely related to that of IST, but it is simpler, largely because it expresses the entropy in terms of normalized probability density functions instead of nonnormalized correlation functions. We show that GTM theory is formally exact for any number of particles, N, whereas IST is not. The unified framework presented here enables thermodynamic mapping of solute and solvent alike and is expected to support a range of applications, including in structure-based drug design, protein design, the analysis of allostery, and materials science. The use of GTM theory to gain insight into protein-ligand binding is illustrated here with an initial case study.

records.title: XL-MS and De Novo Protein Design Identified a Common Motif for TREM2 Binding.
records.abstract: Apolipoprotein E (APOE) and triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) are the two strongest genetic risk factors of late-onset Alzheimer's disease. ApoE binds to the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) to facilitate the uptake of ApoE-lipoprotein particles. TREM2 is a cell surface receptor expressed on microglia in the brain. The activation of TREM2 is essential for microglia to carry out protective functions against AD pathology. Several studies have shown that TREM2 signaling is activated through direct interaction between TREM2 and ApoE. In addition to its important role in AD pathogenesis, the ApoE/TREM2 interaction has been shown to induce immunosuppression of neutrophils within the tumor microenvironment. Despite its clinical importance, a high-resolution molecular understanding of the complex remains elusive. Here, we carried out chemical cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) analysis of the ApoE3/TREM2ECD complex to identify intra- and interprotein cross-links, which were used as restraints to guide integrative protein-protein docking. Our data support a binding model in which a helix-loop-helix motif within the ApoE3 hinge and C-terminal region forms a transient binding pocket that wraps around the hydrophobic tip of the TREM2 ectodomain. This model is further supported by de novo-designed miniprotein binders, which show the same binding mode as identified by our XL-MS experiment. These results establish a robust framework for developing miniprotein-based TREM2 agonists.

records.title: From Isolated Intelligence to Interpretive Infrastructure in Radiology AI.
records.abstract: Radiology has more regulatory-cleared artificial intelligence tools than any other medical specialty, yet they have delivered less consistent clinical impact than their benchmark performance suggested. We argue that the dominant response, scaling perceptual models and extending them toward autonomous agency, mistakes the nature of the problem. The limitation is architectural, not algorithmic: current systems perform isolated perception while remaining disconnected from the temporal, contextual, and experiential integration that interpretation requires. We trace this to a fundamental simulation gap, the absence of the counterfactual signal that lets AI reach superhuman performance in other domains, and argue that scaling alone cannot close it. In response, we outline a hybrid orchestration layer, grounded in established clinical frameworks, that assembles a comprehensive evidence base for the radiologist while keeping generative components constrained and interpretive judgment human. The shift is one of design paradigm: from isolated tools deployed alongside the radiologist to interpretive infrastructure that composes validated outputs into coherent evidence without anchoring the reader's own assessment.
affiliations: Department of Radiology, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY 10065, USA.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in myeloproliferative neoplasms: From digital bone marrow pathology to clinical decision support.
records.abstract: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) are clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders whose diagnosis, prognostication, and management depend on integrating heterogeneous clinical, morphological, and molecular data. This narrative review (PubMed/MEDLINE searched through August 2026, supplemented by hand-searching and conference abstracts) appraises the evidence for AI applications across the MPN continuum. Artificial intelligence (AI), and its principal subfields, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), learn predictive patterns directly from data rather than from explicitly programmed rules, and are increasingly suited to this multidimensional complexity. Across the MPN continuum, AI has produced substantial technical progress across several domains: automated bone marrow biopsy analysis and continuous quantification of fibrosis and megakaryocyte morphology; peripheral blood- and complete blood count-based diagnosis, including blood-based prediction of marrow fibrosis and emerging liquid-biopsy approaches; quantitative disease assessment such as spleen volume segmentation; risk stratification for survival, thrombosis, disease progression, and post-transplant outcomes; therapy response prediction; in silico drug discovery; and natural language processing for large-scale mining of electronic health records; maturity and level of validation differ markedly across these domains. External validation is increasingly reported in selected applications, though most published models to date remain confined to internal or single-cohort validation, and prospective evaluation has been reported only for blood count-based fibrosis prediction. Correspondingly, to our knowledge, no tool has yet been shown to change clinical decision-making or improve patient outcomes, and predictive performance should not be conflated with clinical utility. As multimodal data integration, foundation models, and generative approaches mature, AI has the potential to support a faster, more objective, and more personalized diagnostic and decision-making pathway in MPN.

records.title: Retrospective Analysis of Real-World Elacestrant Use in Two Large Austrian Cancer Centers.
records.abstract: Elacestrant is an oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) approved for the treatment of hormone receptor-positive (HR-positive), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative metastatic breast cancer (MBC) following progression on endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors. While randomized trial data from the EMERALD study demonstrated its clinical benefit, real-world evidence remains limited. We conducted a retrospective chart review of patients with HR-positive/HER2-negative MBC treated with elacestrant at two large cancer centers in Vienna, Austria. Clinical outcomes and safety were evaluated in routine clinical practice by experienced oncologists. Elacestrant demonstrated clinically meaningful efficacy in a heavily pretreated patient population of 30 patients with estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1) mutations. Median age was 65 years and the cohort was predominantly postmenopausal (86.7%). Before initiation of elacestrant, patients had received a median of two lines of endocrine therapy and one line of chemotherapy. Co-mutations of ESR1/PIK3CA were present in 33.3% of patients. Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 3.6 months (95% CI 2.96-4.24) and median overall survival was 20.2 months (95% CI 5.04-35.36). In univariate analyses, de novo metastatic disease and the presence of a single ESR1-mutated exon were associated with longer PFS, whereas the ESR1 E380Q mutation was associated with shorter PFS. Adverse events of any grade occured in 46.7% of patients. Within our cohort, a low rate of dose reductions (3.3%) was found. Subsequent therapies after elacestrant mainly consisted of antibody-drug conjugates (36.7% of patients) and chemotherapy (26.7%). In this real-world cohort, elacestrant showed effectiveness and tolerability similar to data observed in the EMERALD trial. Larger prospective real-world analyses are warranted to further validate these findings and define optimal patient selection.

records.title: Peripheral and selective venous liquid biopsy profiling in localized prostate cancer: A pilot feasibility study.
records.abstract: Liquid biopsy profiling via next-generation sequencing (NGS) is increasingly being used in prostate cancer to identify actionable genomic alterations, monitor disease dynamics, and provide prognostic information. However, the circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) fraction correlates with disease burden, often remaining near the analytical limit of detection in localized disease. Accordingly, strategies to enhance the molecular characterization in earlier-stage disease represent a clinically relevant priority. We conducted a retrospective, single-center observational analysis in a cohort of patients with localized prostate cancer undergoing liquid biopsy. Patients underwent peripheral venous sampling for genomic profiling. When peripheral testing failed to identify genomic alterations or was non-informative, patients proceeded to selective venous blood sampling within the cavo-iliac venous compartment. The primary outcome was the detection rate of reportable genomic alterations in peripheral blood, while exploratory outcomes included findings from selective sampling. Thirty-one patients were enrolled. Peripheral blood liquid biopsy was evaluable in 28 patients. Genomic alterations were detected in 20 of them (20/28, 71.4%; 95% CI, 51.3-86.8%). Patients most frequently harbored mutations in ATM (21.4%), RB1 (14.3%), and BRCA1 or BRCA2 (7.1% each). Eight patients underwent selective venous sampling, with 4 out of 8 (50.0%) demonstrating the presence of at least one genomic alteration. Conversion to mutation-positive occurred in two patients (50.0%) who initially lacked detectable alterations in peripheral blood sampling. Across all available peripheral and selective samples, at least one reportable genomic alteration was identified in 23 of the 31 enrolled patients (74.2%). Our findings demonstrate a high prevalence of genomic mutations in localized prostate cancer. Selective venous sampling was feasible and safe in this small exploratory cohort and provided additional molecular findings in selected patients. These hypothesis-generating data support selective sampling as a potential complementary approach for molecular profiling in localized prostate cancer, deserving prospective validation.

records.title: A Cost-Effective, Kit-Free Method for Extracting Nuclear and Mitochondrial DNA From Low-Abundance Cells in Urine Samples.
records.abstract: This study evaluates a simplified, cost-effective DNA extraction protocol using only 10% sodium chloride (NaCl) and Proteinase K (ProK) to isolate both nuclear DNA (nuDNA) and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) from low-abundance cells in human urine, providing an open-source alternative to expensive commercial kits. Urine samples from six healthy participants were centrifuged, washed with phosphate-buffered saline, lysed with the NaCl/ProK mixture at 60°C overnight, and recovered via ethanol precipitation. To validate downstream applicability, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification was performed targeting the nuclear FGFR3 (423 bp) and the mitochondrial D-loop regions (HV-1: 634 bp, HV-2: 520 bp), followed by agarose gel electrophoresis and Sanger sequencing. The extracted DNA concentrations ranged from undetected to 146.0 μg/mL. PCR amplification of the nuclear FGFR3 succeeded in five out of six samples (83.3%), while the mitochondrial regions (HV-1 and HV-2) achieved a 100% success rate, yielding robust bands even in the sample with undetectable initial genomic DNA. Sanger sequencing and Basic Local Alignment Search Tool search confirmed 100% (FGFR3), 99.4% (HV-1), and 97.8% (HV-2) homology with reference sequences (National Center for Biotechnology Information: NC_012920.1). In conclusion, sequence-ready nuDNA and mtDNA can be successfully extracted using this minimal-reagent, kit-free method. The significantly higher sensitivity of mtDNA highlights its potential for non-invasive genetic diagnostics and point-of-care liquid biopsy in low-biomass specimens.

records.title: Circulating tumor DNA in body fluids for molecular characterization of cancers beyond tissue and blood.
records.abstract: Liquid biopsy using circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is increasingly used for cancer profiling and monitoring, but blood-based analysis may not capture tumor heterogeneity across anatomical compartments. We evaluated cell-free DNA from cerebrospinal (n = 7), pleural (n = 11), pericardial (n = 1), and ascitic (n = 26) fluids from 45 patients with advanced cancer, comparing molecular findings with matched tissue, blood, and cytology where available. Oncogenic alterations were detected in 87% of body fluid samples, with a median variant allele frequency of 3.15%. TP53 (49%), EGFR (18%), and KRAS (18%) were the most frequently altered genes, and ESCAT tier IA alterations occurred in 31.1% of patients. In six patients (13.3%), potentially targetable alterations were detected in body fluids but not in blood and/or tissue. Among five cytology-negative samples, four were ctDNA positive. These findings support body fluid ctDNA profiling as a complementary approach to tissue, plasma, and cytology, thereby warranting prospective validation.
